name: The familiar four-chord loop
description: A bright major-key start moves to the relative minor, then builds through IV to V before resolving back to I.
theory_relationship: All four chords come from the same major scale. The movement alternates stability and lift, with V creating a clear pull toward I.

name: The relative-minor opening
description: Beginning on vi gives the loop a more reflective color before it opens into the major tonic.
theory_relationship: vi shares two notes with I, so it can feel related while changing the emotional starting point. IV and V then lead back toward the home chord.

name: The tonic, subdominant, and dominant
description: This direct route leaves the home chord, increases tension, and returns to the tonic.
theory_relationship: IV moves away from I, while V contains the leading tone that strongly points back to I.

name: The ii–V–I cadence
description: A compact three-chord cadence that moves from preparation, through dominant tension, to resolution.
theory_relationship: The roots descend by fifths (or rise by fourths): ii to V to I. The leading tone in V resolves upward to the tonic.

name: The I–V–vi–IV loop
description: A tonic-and-dominant opening turns toward the relative minor, then settles on IV before repeating.
theory_relationship: The shared major scale keeps the progression cohesive; vi provides contrast after the strong I-to-V motion.

name: The I–vi–ii–V cycle
description: A four-chord cycle that moves from tonic through two related minor chords toward the dominant.
theory_relationship: The roots vi, ii, and V move by descending fifths (or ascending fourths). V then points back to I.

name: The stepwise lift
description: The bass begins at home and climbs through the second and fourth scale degrees before reaching V.
theory_relationship: The rising scale-degree roots create forward motion while every chord remains diatonic to the major key.

name: The descending-fifths chain
description: Four diatonic chords form a smooth chain that can lead into a cadence or continue to I.
theory_relationship: Each root moves by a descending fifth (or ascending fourth), creating a connected path toward the dominant.

name: The minor-to-tonic cadence
description: The progression starts with a relative-minor color and moves through a familiar cadence to the major tonic.
theory_relationship: The roots vi, ii, V, and I form a descending-fifths sequence; the final V-to-I motion gives the clearest resolution.

name: The major-third color
description: A major III adds a bright chromatic lift between the home chord and the relative minor.
theory_relationship: In C major, E major is E–G#–B: G# is outside the C-major scale. That raised note gives III a distinct color before Am.

name: The chromatic lift to IV
description: A major III creates a chromatic lift before the progression opens onto IV.
theory_relationship: In C major, E major contains G# instead of the scale's G natural. The raised third adds a bright, unexpected color before F major.

name: The minor-five return
description: A minor v gives the dominant chord a softer, darker sound before I moves to IV.
theory_relationship: In C major, G minor uses Bb rather than the scale's B natural. The lowered seventh softens the usual dominant pull into C.

name: The major-two step
description: A major II gives the step away from I a brighter, more lifted quality before IV.
theory_relationship: In C major, D major contains F# instead of the scale's F natural. That raised fourth creates the major II color before F major.
